notes.definition: The balancing numbers (coefficients) in a symbol equation can be calculated from the masses of reactants and products that react, by converting each mass in grams into an amount in moles and then converting the numbers of moles into a simple whole number ratio.
explanation: Usually you balance an equation by counting atoms. But you can also work out the balancing numbers from experimental data. If you know the masses of all the reactants and products involved in a reaction, you can find how many moles of each took part. The coefficients in a balanced equation are simply the simplest whole number ratio of these numbers of moles.

The method has four steps. Step 1: write down the mass of each substance. Step 2: convert each mass into moles using moles = mass ÷ Mr. Step 3: divide every number of moles by the smallest number of moles. Step 4: if any of the results are not whole numbers, multiply them all by the same small number (for example 2) to make them whole. These whole numbers are the coefficients in the balanced equation.

For example, 4.8 g of magnesium reacts with 3.2 g of oxygen to make 8.0 g of magnesium oxide. Moles: Mg = 4.8 ÷ 24 = 0.20, O₂ = 3.2 ÷ 32 = 0.10, MgO = 8.0 ÷ 40 = 0.20. Dividing by the smallest (0.10) gives 2 : 1 : 2, so the equation is 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. Remember to use the Mr of the formula as it appears in the equation: O₂ has Mr 32, not 16.

Sometimes dividing by the smallest gives a ratio such as 1 : 1.5 : 1. You cannot have half a coefficient, so multiply everything by 2 to give 2 : 3 : 2. For example, iron reacting with chlorine to form iron(III) chloride gives a mole ratio Fe : Cl₂ : FeCl₃ of 1 : 1.5 : 1, which becomes 2Fe + 3Cl₂ → 2FeCl₃.

If one mass is missing, use the law of conservation of mass first: the total mass of reactants equals the total mass of products. Then carry on with the method. Always finish by counting atoms in your equation to check that it really is balanced. This method links experimental results to the theory of balanced equations, and is how chemists confirm the formulae and ratios in new reactions.
keyFacts: Coefficients in a balanced equation are the simplest whole number ratio of moles.
Step 1: write down the mass of each reactant and product.
Step 2: convert each mass to moles: moles = mass ÷ Mr.
Step 3: divide all the mole values by the smallest one.
Step 4: if needed, multiply all values by the same number to make whole numbers.
Use the Mr of the formula exactly as written in the equation (O₂ = 32, H₂ = 2, Cl₂ = 71).
A missing mass can be found using conservation of mass before you start.
Always check your final equation by counting atoms of each element.

keyTerms.definition: The ratio of the numbers of moles of the substances that react and are produced.
A ratio in which all the numbers are whole and cannot be divided by a common factor.
A balancing number written in front of a formula in an equation.
The sum of the relative atomic masses of the atoms in a formula.
The total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants.
A molecule made of two atoms, such as O₂, H₂, N₂ or Cl₂.

equations.name: Number of moles
equations.formula: number of moles = mass in grams ÷ relative formula mass
equations.units: n in mol, m in g

workedExamples.title: A simple 2 : 1 : 2 ratio
workedExamples.question: 4.8 g of magnesium reacts with 3.2 g of oxygen to make 8.0 g of magnesium oxide. Use these masses to write a balanced equation. (Ar: O = 16, Mg = 24)
steps: Divide by the smallest (0.10): Mg 2, O₂ 1, MgO 2.

workedExamples.title: Making a ratio whole
workedExamples.question: 11.2 g of iron reacts with 21.3 g of chlorine to make 32.5 g of iron(III) chloride, FeCl₃. Write the balanced equation. (Ar: Cl = 35.5, Fe = 56)
steps: Multiply by 2 to make whole numbers: 2 : 3 : 2.

workedExamples.title: Finding a missing mass first
workedExamples.question: 1.6 g of methane burns in 6.4 g of oxygen to give 4.4 g of carbon dioxide and some water. Calculate the mass of water and write the balanced equation. (Ar: H = 1, C = 12, O = 16)
steps: Conservation of mass: mass of water = (1.6 + 6.4) − 4.4 = 3.6 g.

diagrams.title: From masses to a balanced equation
diagrams.caption: A table method for the reaction of 2.8 g of nitrogen with 0.6 g of hydrogen to make 3.4 g of ammonia. The mole ratio 1 : 3 : 2 gives N₂ + 3H₂ → 2NH₃.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often use the Ar of oxygen (16) when finding the moles of oxygen gas.
misconceptions.right: In fact oxygen gas is O₂, so use Mr = 32. The Mr must match the formula in the equation.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often stop at a ratio such as 1 : 1.5 : 1 and write 1.5 as a coefficient.
misconceptions.right: In fact coefficients must be whole numbers, so multiply every value by 2 to get 2 : 3 : 2.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the mass ratio gives the coefficients directly.
misconceptions.right: In fact masses must be converted to moles first, because different substances have different Mr values.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often divide each number of moles by a different number to make them whole.
misconceptions.right: In fact you must divide all of them by the same (smallest) value, so the ratio is unchanged.

realWorld: Chemists use reacting masses to work out the equation for a new reaction, which is needed before the process can be scaled up in industry.
Analytical chemists find the formulae of new compounds, such as medicines, by measuring the masses that react and converting them to mole ratios.
Quality control laboratories check that products are made in the expected ratio by comparing measured masses with those predicted by the equation.
higherTier: This whole subtopic is Higher tier only: balancing an equation from the masses of reactants and products by converting masses to moles and finding the simplest whole number ratio.
examTips: Set out your working as a table with a row for mass, moles and ratio; it is clear and earns method marks.
Check the formula of each gas: O₂, H₂, N₂ and Cl₂ are diatomic, so use their Mr values.
If a mass is not given, find it with conservation of mass before converting to moles.
If you get 1.5 or 2.5 in a ratio, multiply everything by 2; if you get 1.33, multiply by 3.
Finish by counting atoms on both sides: a quick check that catches most errors.
summary: Balancing numbers can be found from reacting masses.
Convert each mass to moles using moles = mass ÷ Mr.
Divide all values by the smallest number of moles.
Multiply by a small number if needed to make whole numbers.
Use Mr of formulae exactly as written (O₂ = 32).
Check the final equation by counting atoms.

flashcards.front: What are the steps to balance an equation from reacting masses?
flashcards.back: Convert masses to moles, divide by the smallest, multiply to make whole numbers if needed, use as coefficients.

questions.question:
A student uses the masses of reactants and products to balance an equation.
What should the student do first?
options: Divide each mass by the smallest mass
markScheme: 1 mark: convert each mass into moles
questions.explanation: Coefficients are mole ratios, so you must convert masses to moles (mass ÷ Mr) before finding the ratio.

questions.question:
A student has calculated the amount in moles of each substance in a reaction.
Which value should the student divide all the amounts by?
markScheme: 1 mark: the smallest number of moles
questions.explanation: Dividing by the smallest value makes the smallest number 1 and gives the simplest ratio.

questions.question:
A student calculates the amount in moles of chlorine gas, Cl₂, from its mass.
Which relative formula mass (Mr) should the student use?
Relative atomic mass (Ar): Cl = 35.5
questions.explanation: Chlorine gas is diatomic, Cl₂, so Mr = 2 × 35.5 = 71.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the amounts of substances A, B and C in a reaction.
What is the simplest whole number ratio A : B : C?
questions.explanation: Divide each by the smallest (0.15): 1 : 2 : 1. 15 : 30 : 15 is the same ratio but not the simplest.

questions.question:
A student divides the amount of each substance in a reaction by the smallest amount. This gives the ratio 1 : 1.5 : 1.
Which numbers should the student use to balance the equation?
questions.explanation: Multiply all values by 2 to remove the half: 2 : 3 : 2. Rounding 1.5 to 1 or 2 would change the ratio.

questions.question:
Nitrogen reacts with hydrogen to produce ammonia.
Table 1 shows the masses in one reaction.
What is the balanced equation for the reaction?
Relative atomic masses (Ar): H = 1; N = 14
questions.explanation: Moles: N₂ 0.1, H₂ 0.3, NH₃ 0.2, giving 1 : 3 : 2. N₂ + 6H₂ → 4NH₃ is not balanced (N 2 compared with 4).

questions.question:
Magnesium reacts with oxygen:
2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO
A student uses reacting masses to find the ratio Mg : O₂. The student wrongly uses Mr = 16 for oxygen gas.
What ratio Mg : O₂ will the student get?
questions.explanation: Using 16 instead of 32 doubles the calculated moles of oxygen, changing the true 2 : 1 into 2 : 2, which is 1 : 1.

questions.question:
Sodium reacts with oxygen to produce sodium oxide.
Table 1 shows the masses in one reaction.
What is the balanced equation for the reaction?
Relative atomic masses (Ar): O = 16; Na = 23
questions.explanation: Moles: Na 0.4, O₂ 0.1, Na₂O 0.2, giving 4 : 1 : 2. Check: Na 4 = 4, O 2 = 2.

questions.question:
A student divides the amount of each substance in a reaction by the smallest amount. This gives the ratio 1 : 1.33 : 1.
What number should the student multiply all the values by?
questions.explanation: 1.33 is about 4 ÷ 3, so multiplying by 3 gives 3 : 4 : 3, all whole numbers.

questions.question:
Calculate the amount in moles of oxygen gas, O₂, in 3.2 g of oxygen.
Relative atomic mass (Ar): O = 16
questions.explanation: Use Mr of O₂ = 32. Using 16 would give 0.20 mol, which is wrong.

questions.question:
Calculate the amount in moles of aluminium atoms in 5.4 g of aluminium.
Relative atomic mass (Ar): Al = 27
questions.explanation: moles = mass ÷ Ar for an element: 5.4 ÷ 27 = 0.20 mol.

questions.question:
Methane burns in oxygen to produce carbon dioxide and water.
Table 1 shows the masses in one reaction.
Calculate the mass of water produced.
questions.explanation: Mass is conserved: total reactants 8.0 g = 4.4 g + mass of water, so water = 3.6 g.

questions.question:
Aluminium reacts with chlorine to produce aluminium chloride, AlCl₃.
Table 1 shows the masses in one reaction.
In the balanced equation the balancing number for Al is 2.
Calculate the balancing number for Cl₂.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): Al = 27; Cl = 35.5
markScheme: 1 mark: × 2 gives 2 : 3, so coefficient of Cl₂ = 3
questions.explanation: The ratio Al : Cl₂ = 0.20 : 0.30 = 2 : 3, so the equation is 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃.

questions.question:
Calculate the amount in moles of carbon dioxide in 13.2 g of carbon dioxide, CO₂.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): C = 12; O = 16
questions.explanation: Mr of CO₂ = 44, so 13.2 ÷ 44 = 0.30 mol.

questions.question:
Copper reacts with oxygen to produce copper oxide, CuO.
Table 1 shows the masses in one reaction.
In the balanced equation the balancing number for O₂ is 1.
Calculate the balancing number for CuO.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): O = 16; Cu = 63.5
markScheme: 1 mark: ratio 2 : 1 : 2, so coefficient of CuO = 2
questions.explanation: The balanced equation is 2Cu + O₂ → 2CuO.

questions.question:
Propane, C₃H₈, burns in oxygen to produce carbon dioxide and water.
Table 1 shows the masses in one reaction.
Use the data to find the balancing number for O₂ in the balanced equation.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): H = 1; C = 12; O = 16
markScheme: 1 mark: Mr values C₃H₈ 44, O₂ 32, CO₂ 44, H₂O 18
questions.explanation: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O. Check: C 3 = 3, H 8 = 8, O 10 = 6 + 4.

questions.question:
Iron(III) oxide reacts with carbon monoxide to produce iron and carbon dioxide.
Table 1 shows the masses in one reaction.
Calculate the balancing number for CO in the balanced equation.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): C = 12; O = 16; Fe = 56
markScheme: 1 mark: ratio 1 : 3 : 2 : 3, so coefficient of CO = 3
questions.explanation: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂.

questions.question: Explain why masses must be converted into moles before working out the balancing numbers in an equation.
markScheme: 1 mark: the coefficients show the ratio of particles (moles)
1 mark: different substances have different Mr, so equal masses do not contain equal numbers of particles
questions.explanation: 1 g of hydrogen contains far more molecules than 1 g of oxygen, so mass ratios are not particle ratios.

questions.question:
The amounts of the reactants and product in a reaction are in the ratio 0.2 : 0.1 : 0.2.
Give the simplest whole number ratio.
questions.explanation: Divide every value by the smallest, 0.1.

questions.question:
Carbon reacts with oxygen to produce carbon dioxide.
Table 1 shows the masses in one reaction.
Use the masses to show that the balanced equation is C + O₂ → CO₂
Relative atomic masses (Ar): C = 12; O = 16
markScheme: 1 mark: ratio 1 : 1 : 1, so C + O₂ → CO₂
questions.explanation: All three are 0.10 mol, so the ratio is 1 : 1 : 1.

questions.question:
Magnesium reacts with oxygen to produce magnesium oxide, MgO.
Table 1 shows the masses in one reaction.
Use the masses to write a balanced equation for the reaction.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): O = 16; Mg = 24
questions.explanation: Divide each by 0.10 to get 2 : 1 : 2.

questions.question:
Iron reacts with chlorine to produce iron chloride, FeCl₃.
Table 1 shows the masses in one reaction.
Use the masses to write the balanced equation for the reaction.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): Cl = 35.5; Fe = 56
questions.explanation: The ratio contains 1.5, so multiply every value by 2 to make whole numbers.

questions.question:
A student finds the mole ratio Fe : Cl₂ : FeCl₃ = 1 : 1.5 : 1
The student writes the equation:
Fe + 1.5Cl₂ → FeCl₃
Explain what is wrong with the equation.
Write the correct balanced equation.
markScheme: 1 mark: balancing numbers should be whole numbers (cannot have half a molecule in the ratio)
questions.explanation: Multiplying every coefficient by the same number keeps the ratio the same and gives whole numbers.

questions.question:
Give the relative formula mass (Mr) you would use for hydrogen gas to calculate an amount in moles.
Relative atomic mass (Ar): H = 1
questions.explanation: Hydrogen gas is made of H₂ molecules, so Mr = 2 × 1 = 2.

questions.question: Describe how to work out a balanced equation from the masses of all the reactants and products in a reaction.
markScheme: Indicative content: if any mass is missing, find it using conservation of mass; calculate Mr of each substance using the formula as written (for example O₂ = 32); convert each mass to moles using moles = mass ÷ Mr; divide all mole values by the smallest; if not all whole numbers, multiply all by the same number (for example 2 or 3); use these as coefficients; check by counting atoms.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a complete, logically ordered method including dividing by the smallest and making whole numbers.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct steps, for example converting masses to moles, but incomplete.
questions.explanation: The core steps are mass → moles → divide by smallest → whole numbers → coefficients, finishing with an atom check.

questions.question:
A student heats copper oxide in a stream of hydrogen gas.
Figure 1 shows the apparatus.
The copper oxide is reduced to copper and water is produced.
Table 1 shows the student's results.
Use the data to work out:
• the mass of water produced
• the formula of the copper oxide, by finding the mass of oxygen in it
• the balanced equation for the reaction.
Explain each step.
Relative atomic masses (Ar): H = 1; O = 16; Cu = 63.5

markScheme: Indicative content: mass of oxygen in copper oxide = 7.95 − 6.35 = 1.60 g; moles Cu = 6.35 ÷ 63.5 = 0.10; moles O = 1.60 ÷ 16 = 0.10; ratio 1 : 1 so formula CuO; mass of water = (7.95 + 0.20) − 6.35 = 1.80 g; moles: CuO = 7.95 ÷ 79.5 = 0.10, H₂ = 0.20 ÷ 2 = 0.10, Cu = 0.10, H₂O = 1.80 ÷ 18 = 0.10; ratio 1 : 1 : 1 : 1; CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O; check atoms Cu 1, O 1, H 2 on each side.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): all three parts correct with clear explanations and correct use of conservation of mass and mole ratios.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): two parts correct, or all attempted with minor errors.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one part correct, for example the mass of water or oxygen, with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Conservation of mass gives the oxygen (1.60 g) and the water (1.80 g). Converting each mass to moles gives equal amounts, so the oxide is CuO and the equation is CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O.
